title: More Layers, More Plants: The Counterintuitive Science of Staying Cool
summary:
When summer heat waves hit, the instinct is to strip down to shorts and a tank top. But science says that might be making you hotter. As global temperatures climb—the last three years were the hottest on record—knowing how to stay cool is crucial. Thousands die annually from heat-related illness, which occurs when the body's core temperature rises dangerously. Sweating normally cools us, but high humidity slows evaporation, leading to symptoms like headaches, vomiting, and fainting.

Roxana Chicas, an environmental health scientist at Emory University, emphasizes that outdoor workers, young children, and athletes are especially vulnerable. But innovative, research-backed strategies can help anyone beat the heat without staying indoors.

One surprising tactic: wear more clothing. "Just one layer of clothing reduces the impact of those rays to help you stay cooler," says Asis Patnaik, a textile researcher at Cape Peninsula University of Technology. Direct sunlight heats bare skin faster. Loose, natural-fiber garments like cotton or linen allow sweat to wick away and evaporate, cooling the skin. In extreme heat regions like the Middle East, people wear multiple loose layers; the air gaps act as insulators, keeping hot outer fabric away from the body.

Plants are another powerful tool. Green spaces are consistently cooler because trees provide shade and release moisture through their leaves—a process called transpiration. A 2024 study in India found that a balcony with potted plants was 3.3°C (5.9°F) cooler than a bare one, and indoor temperatures dropped by 2.3°C (4.1°F). Window boxes offer similar benefits, shading windows and reducing heat entering the home. Even with air conditioning, plants can cut energy use.

These simple, natural methods can make summer safer and more enjoyable. As Chicas notes, "We think that the sun is fun, but it can also be very dangerous." With a few adjustments, you can have both.
why_it_matters: As climate change intensifies heat waves, understanding affordable, natural cooling methods becomes essential for protecting health and reducing reliance on energy-intensive air conditioning, which contributes to global warming. These strategies empower young people to keep themselves and their families safer during increasingly hot summers.

background_read: Extreme heat is the deadliest weather-related hazard in the United States, killing more people each year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. Climate change has made heat waves more frequent and intense; the last eight years were the warmest on record globally.

Roxana Chicas (an environmental health scientist at Emory University in Atlanta) studies how outdoor workers, such as agricultural laborers, are disproportionately affected because they cannot easily escape the sun. Her work shows that simple interventions—like resting in shaded areas and wearing appropriate clothing—can save lives.

Meanwhile, textile researcher Asis Patnaik of Cape Peninsula University of Technology (in South Africa) investigates how clothing design influences thermal comfort. Traditional garments in the Middle East, such as the loose-fitting thobe or abaya, have long demonstrated the counterintuitive benefit of layers: air trapped between fabric and skin provides insulation from outside heat.

Finally, the cooling power of plants is not new; urban planners have been incorporating 'green infrastructure' to reduce the urban heat island effect, where cities can be up to 7°F warmer than surrounding rural areas.

perspectives.description: More clothing and plants offer simple, low-cost solutions that anyone can adopt, making heat waves more bearable without expensive technology. They reduce energy use and can be implemented in homes, schools, and communities almost anywhere.

These methods alone may not be sufficient during extreme heat events for people who work outdoors or lack safe housing; they aren't a substitute for systemic solutions like better access to air-conditioned shelters. Relying solely on these could give a false sense of security.

The science behind layering and transpiration reflects long-understood principles of thermal physics and physiology. However, behavioral change is slow, and many people continue to think stripping down is the only way to cope, suggesting a gap between research and public awareness.

As cities invest in green spaces and 'cool roof' initiatives, the combination of personal behavior and urban planning could make heat waves less deadly. More research is needed on how to protect the most vulnerable, such as outdoor workers, during ever-hotter summers.
